questions.stem: Which of the following provides the best evidence for the influence of heredity as opposed to environment?

options.A: Fraternal twins have more similar interests than typical siblings.
options.B: Identical twins raised together score less similarly on intelligence tests than identical twins raised separately.
options.C: Fraternal twins raised together score more similarly on intelligence tests than fraternal twins raised separately.
options.D: Identical twins raised separately tend to resemble their birth parents more than their adoptive parents.

questions.answer_text: Identical twins raised separately tend to resemble their birth parents more than their adoptive parents in many ways, which suggests that genetics plays a stronger role than the family environment. Identical twins share 100 percent of their genetic material, so differences between them are attributed to their environments. Because, on average, fraternal twins share the same amount of genetic material as siblings born at different times, any greater similarity between them must be due to environmental factors. Likewise, given that fraternal twins share an average of 50 percent of their genes, differences between them are likely due to the environment.

questions.stem: Psychologists have long debated the relative influence of nature and nurture. Which of the following statements provides the strongest evidence in support of the influence of nature?

options.A: Identical twins raised separately often exhibit striking similarities in personality.
options.B: Identical twins raised together often exhibit striking similarities in personality.
options.C: Fraternal twins raised together often exhibit striking similarities in personality.
options.D: Fraternal twins raised separately often exhibit striking similarities in personality.

questions.answer_text: Since identical twins share 100 percent of their genetic material, when identical twins are raised in separate environments, psychological researchers are very interested in looking at their similarities and differences. Whatever is similar between identical twins raised in separate environments may be largely influenced by genetics since they share the same genetic code (nature) but experienced different environments (nurture). Fraternal twins aren’t as useful as identical twins for this kind of research because they don’t share as similar a genetic code as identical twins.

questions.stem: The study design used by Dr. Perez would be classified as
questions.context: Use the following information to answer questions 3 and 4. Dr. Perez and her research assistant are interested in how extraversion changes over the lifespan. Over the course of several months, they survey 40 people in their early teens, 40 people in their early 30’s, and 40 people in their early 50’s, and they use this data to make comparisons across cohorts of different ages.
questions.answer_text: Developmental psychology researchers who use the cross- sectional research method typically gather a large group of participants and compare the same variable (such as extraversion) between groups based on age. They obviously can’t randomly assign people to different age groups (which would be required in a true experiment). Meta-analysis is a research technique that combines statistical data across many different studies. True longitudinal studies study the same group of people over a long period of years (which was not done in Dr. Perez’s study).

questions.stem: Which of the following is likely to be the biggest issue in Dr. Perez’s study?

options.A: Participants may drop out midway through the study.
options.B: Ten years is not enough time for extraversion to change.
options.C: Differences between groups may be due to factors other than age.
options.D: Surveys are not appropriate tools with which to answer this question.

questions.context: Use the following information to answer questions 3 and 4. Dr. Perez and her research assistant are interested in how extraversion changes over the lifespan. Over the course of several months, they survey 40 people in their early teens, 40 people in their early 30’s, and 40 people in their early 50’s, and they use this data to make comparisons across cohorts of different ages.
questions.answer_text: One of the limitations of cross sectional studies (and any nonexperimental study that can’t use random assignment to groups) is that there may be differences between the groups other than the variable researchers want to study (confounding variables). Answers A, B, and D may turn out to be issues with Dr. Perez’s study, but they are not necessarily issues unique to the cross sectional method used in this research, and they are not more likely to be issues in this study than other research.

questions.stem: A deer runs into the road while Harry is driving, and he has to swerve and hit the brakes. As he slows to a stop, Harry’s heart is pounding and his breathing rate is elevated. Harry’s reaction is controlled by the
questions.answer_text: Harry’s reaction is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system. The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems make up the autonomic nervous system, which controls our involuntary actions. The sympathetic nervous system prepares us to react to stressful situations, while the parasympathetic symptom calms us back down after the threat has passed.

questions.stem: Shortly after birth, Katerina’s pediatrician refers her to a specialist because he is concerned about her reflexes. Which part of the nervous system is the doctor probably least worried about?
questions.answer_text: As Katerina’s pediatrician explores potential physiological issues that might be causing Katerina’s reflex issues, they are unlikely to start with the cerebral cortex as the root cause because reflex actions are controlled in the spinal cord (see “reflex arcs”), not the cerebral cortex. Katerina’s pediatrician is more likely to explore potential problems in the motor neurons, sensory neurons, and peripheral nervous system than the cerebral cortex.

questions.stem: A drug that blocks the perception of pain is most likely to be

options.D: a glutamate antagonist. Use this diagram for items 8–10.

questions.answer_text: Endorphins are the body’s natural painkillers. Agonists mimic the effect of other compounds; thus, an endorphin agonist would decrease the perception of pain.

questions.stem: In the diagram, X represents one neuron and Y represents another neuron. The process depicted in the diagram would best be described as
questions.answer_text: The diagram focuses on transfer of neurotransmitters across the synaptic gap. This is a chemical process, not an electrical one (action potentials operate within a neuron, not across the synaptic gap). Correlation (a research method) and Evolutionary perspective (a psychological perspective related to the biological perspective) are not specifically related to neural transmission across the synaptic gap.

questions.stem: Which of the following could be represented by the small circles in the diagram including those indicated by letter E?
questions.answer_text: Answer B, Acetylcholine, is the only answer choice that is a neurotransmitter (leptin, testosterone, and cortisol are hormones). The letter E in the diagram is referring to neurotransmitters crossing the synaptic gap, so the answer must be a neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: The area in the diagram marked by C is referred to as the
questions.answer_text: The area in the diagram marked by C refers to the space between neuron X and neuron Y. This space is called the “synaptic gap” or simply the synapse. Answer choices A, B, and C are individual parts of a neuron, not the gap between neurons.

questions.stem: Antonia goes to the doctor complaining of tiredness and periods when she feels numbness and tingling in various parts of her body. She tells the doctor that she has also been feeling weak and having trouble with her balance. The doctor sends her for an MRI to test whether she is suffering from a loss of myelination in her neurons. What is the doctor likely concerned about?
questions.answer_text: Multiple sclerosis is associated with the deterioration of the myelin sheath in brain neurons because patient’s immune systems begin to mistakenly attack myelin cells. Myelin deterioration is not commonly associated with schizophrenia, Alzheimer’s disease, or Myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: Dr. Dahab, a brain researcher, is investigating the connection between certain environmental stimuli and brain processes. Which types of brain scans is he most likely to use?
questions.answer_text: The PET and EEG scans both give information about brain function. (The PET measures brain activity, and the EEG measures brain waves.) The MRI and CAT scans give information about brain structure, not function. An EKG is a medical test for heart function.

questions.stem: Split-brain patients are unable to

options.A: coordinate movements between their major and minor muscle groups.
options.B: speak about information received exclusively in their right hemisphere.
options.C: speak about information received exclusively in their left hemisphere.
options.D: solve abstract problems involving integrating logical (left- hemisphere) and spatial (right-hemisphere) information.

questions.answer_text: Since the left hemisphere typically controls speech, split- brain patients are usually unable to talk about information exposed to only the right hemisphere. Their muscle coordination is usually normal (possible after a short adjustment period). Their ability to solve abstract problems is not affected.

questions.stem: Mr. Spam is a 39-year-old male who has been brought into your neurology clinic by his wife. She has become increasingly alarmed by her husband’s behavior over the last four months. You recommend a CAT scan to look for tumors in the brain. Which two parts of the brain would you predict are being affected by the tumors? List of symptoms: vastly increased appetite, body temperature fluctuations, decreased sexual desire, jerky movements, poor balance when walking and standing, inability to throw objects, and exaggerated efforts to coordinate movements in a task
questions.answer_text: A tumor on the hypothalamus would explain the first three symptoms since the hypothalamus controls (at least in part) body temperature, libido, and hunger. The cerebellum coordinates some types of movements, including throwing objects and our sense of balance. The motor cortex controls voluntary muscle movements, but the specific movements described in the question are controlled by the cerebellum. The medulla controls our life-support functions, like heart rate and respiration.

questions.stem: After being in a car accident, Suzy is having difficulty with her vision. Which part of her brain is most likely to have been affected?
questions.answer_text: The thalamus is the relay station for all sensory information except for smell. Information coming from the optic nerve is routed to the lateral geniculate nucleus in the thalamus and then on to the occipital lobe of the brain. Suzy is having difficulty with her vision most likely because her thalamus was affected by the car accident.

questions.stem: After a minor stroke, Jeri is having difficulty moving her left arm and hand, and she has also been struggling with identifying items when she closes her eyes and feels them with her left hand. Which parts of the brain did the stroke most likely damage?
questions.answer_text: Jeri’s brain issue is clearly focused in the right hemisphere, since all the reported symptoms involve movement with her left arm or hand, so choices A and B are incorrect. The symptoms include difficulty in sensing touch information from the left hand (sensorimotor cortex, parietal lobe) and moving the left hand and arm (motor cortex, frontal lobe). There is no indication of vision or hearing issues, which rules out option D.

questions.stem: Kate’s cat Wilma seems unable to relax. Even after living with Kate in the same quiet apartment for years, Wilma remains nearly constantly vigilant. Which part of Wilma’s brain likely accounts for this aspect of her personality?
questions.answer_text: The reticular formation is a brain structure directly above the spinal cord, deep within the brain, that is directly involved in attention and arousal. An issue with this brain structure might help explain Wilma the cat’s “vigilance” behaviors. The other brain structures are less likely to be involved: the thalamus controls basic “life support” functions, the pons is involved with sleep/wake cycles, and the hippocampus is primarily involved in memory.

questions.stem: Bertrand falls asleep at unusual times, including in the middle of arguments. With which disorder is he most likely to be diagnosed?
questions.answer_text: Narcolepsy typically involves falling asleep at unusual, often stressful, times. Sleep apnea is characterized by waking up in the middle of the night and struggling to breathe, insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep, and somnambulism is sleepwalking.

In his university lab, 40 students from his Introduction to Psychology class are randomly assigned either to a control condition in which they are left to sleep without disruption or to a REM deprivation condition in which they are awakened every time an EEG indicates that they are entering REM. The students report to the lab directly after Dr. Webb’s class on Monday, and at the next class meeting, they take a quiz on the material taught Monday. The graph below shows the results of the study.
questions.answer_text: Memory is a cognitive function. Therefore, the finding that depriving people of REM sleep interferes with the memory of information taught suggests that REM sleep has a cognitive function.

questions.stem: The biggest ethical concern associated with Dr. Webb’s study would be
questions.context: Questions 2 through 4 refer to the following. Dr. Webb is studying what happens when people are deprived of REM sleep. In his university lab, 40 students from his Introduction to Psychology class are randomly assigned either to a control condition in which they are left to sleep without disruption or to a REM deprivation condition in which they are awakened every time an EEG indicates that they are entering REM. The students report to the lab directly after Dr. Webb’s class on Monday, and at the next class meeting, they take a quiz on the material taught Monday. The graph below shows the results of the study.
questions.answer_text: Given that Dr. Webb is experimenting on his own students, he needs to be especially concerned about their ability to freely consent (or not) to their participation. As he is their professor, they may feel some pressure to agree to be in the study. Dr. Webb would therefore need to make clear that their participation or lack thereof will have no effect on their performance in his class or on their relationship with him outside of the class.

questions.stem: If Dr. Webb wants to generalize his findings beyond his sample, it would be most valuable for him to

options.A: test these students again later in the semester.
options.B: test students from a class he will teach the following semester.
options.C: test students of different ages from a variety of schools.
options.D: test students from a variety of colleges and classes.

In his university lab, 40 students from his Introduction to Psychology class are randomly assigned either to a control condition in which they are left to sleep without disruption or to a REM deprivation condition in which they are awakened every time an EEG indicates that they are entering REM. The students report to the lab directly after Dr. Webb’s class on Monday, and at the next class meeting, they take a quiz on the material taught Monday. questions.answer_text: Although all the replications mentioned would be useful, if Dr. Webb wants to make the argument that REM sleep is important for learning and remembering information in a broader population than college students, choice (C) is the best method.

questions.stem: The chart below depicts a man named James’ sleep over the course of one night. Use the chart to answer the following questions. Over the course of the night, this person spent the least amount of time in which stage?
questions.answer_text: The graph shows that James spent the least amount of time, about 1–1.5 hours, in non-REM 3 sleep (marked “N3” in the graph). James spent the most amount of time in non-REM 2 sleep (“N2” in the graph).

questions.stem: A psychologist monitoring James’ sleep would be most likely to see sleep spindles during which stage of sleep?
questions.answer_text: Sleep Spindles are specific patterns of brain waves that are detected during an EEG scan. Sleep spindles may occur in any stages of non-REM sleep, but they are most prevalent in stage 2 (non-REM 2).

questions.stem: In order to determine which stage of sleep James was in over the course of the night, the psychologists monitoring James would be most likely to make use of
questions.answer_text: EEG scans measure brain wave activity, and that is the most likely technology a psychologist would use to monitor James’s brain activity during sleep. PET scans also can measure brain activity but are usually “one time” scans used to take a snapshot of brain activity at a specific moment, while EEG scans can be more easily continuously used over a long period of time (such as an entire night of sleep). MRI scans are used to examine brain structure, not activity. EMG scans are used to detect electrical activity in specific muscles, not brain waves.

questions.stem: What is the principal difference between amplitude and frequency in the context of sound waves?

options.A: Amplitude is the tone or timbre of a sound, whereas frequency is the pitch.
options.B: Amplitude is detected in the cochlea, whereas frequency is detected in the auditory cortex.
options.C: Amplitude is the height of the sound wave, whereas frequency is a measure of how frequently the sound waves pass a given point.
options.D: Both measure qualities of sound, but frequency is a more accurate measure since it measures the shapes of the waves rather than the strength of the waves.

questions.answer_text: Amplitude is a measure of the height of the wave, creating the volume of the sound. Frequency is the measure of how quickly the waves pass a point, causing the pitch of the sound. The other choices are incorrect distractions.

questions.stem: What behavior would be difficult without our vestibular sense?

options.A: Integrating what we see and hear
options.D: Walking a straight line with our eyes closed

questions.answer_text: Our vestibular sense helps with our sense of balance and orientation in space. Our vestibular sense has little to do with our sense of sight or hearing. Repeating digits would not be affected by the vestibular sense.

questions.stem: How do chemical senses differ from energy senses?

options.A: People need to interact more closely with a chemical stimulus sense.
options.B: The chemical senses are more important to most people than the energy senses.
options.C: More research has focused on chemical senses than on energy senses.
options.D: More of the brain is devoted to processing chemical sensation than energy sensation.

questions.answer_text: Chemical senses include smell and taste. To smell or taste things, they need to come into contact with our receptors—our olfactory and taste cells. Vision, which is an energy sense, is thought of as humans’ dominant sense. Because most humans rely on their vision more than their other senses, more research has been done on vision and more of the brain’s real estate is devoted to processing this energy sense.

questions.stem: Eli plays percussion in a band. He’s been urged to wear earplugs in order to protect his hearing. Which part of the ear is most likely to be protected by earplugs?
questions.answer_text: Hair cells are the receptors for hearing, which means they are where transduction (the conversion of one form of energy to another) takes place. Although it is not impossible to damage the ossicles (bones in the middle ear) or tympanic membrane (ear drum) with loud noise, this type of hearing loss is usually caused by damage to the hair cells. The pinna, the outer part of the ear, is not damaged by noise.

questions.stem: Dr. Simons studies the relationship between the various senses. The results of her most recent study are graphed in the scatter plot below. Which of the following statements best summarizes the data in the chart?

options.A: Both vision and hearing decline after age 65.
options.B: People with poor vision tend to make up for it with better hearing.
options.C: Deficits in vision lead to similar deficits in hearing.
options.D: The participants with better hearing tended to have better vision.

questions.answer_text: The scatter plot indicates at least a slightly positive correlation between auditory acuity and visual acuity (the “trend line” or line of best fit for this scatter plot would travel from the lower left part of the graph toward the upper right). A positive correlation between two variables indicates that as one variable increases, the other variable tends to increase. Therefore, option D is the correct answer. Option A includes information about age which is not represented in the scatter plot. Options B and C refer to a causal relationship between the two variables, and correlational data cannot be used to infer cause.

questions.stem: At a birthday party, the host has children play a game where they need to identify common objects like a comb and a set of dice while blindfolded and using only the back of their hands. What makes this task difficult?

options.A: The neurons that identify objects by touch are only located in our fingertips.
options.B: Our sense of touch depends on our ability to see the objects we are touching.
options.C: Children are less familiar with many common objects than are adults.
options.D: We have far fewer somatosensory receptors in the back of our hands than in the front.

questions.answer_text: The specialized neurons in our skin that detect touch sensations are concentrated in the parts of our body that are the most “sensitive” to touch, such as our fingertips and lips. These touch receptors are not concentrated in many other areas of our body, including the backs of our hands. Options A and B are factually incorrect statements, and option C may be true for some children, but all the objects in the game were common objects, so this point is irrelevant.

questions.stem: If you had sight in only one eye, which of the following depth cues could you NOT use?
questions.answer_text: All the other choices are monocular cues for depth, so they could be used by a person sighted in only one eye. Convergence is a binocular cue and does not work without two functioning eyes. When an object is close to our face and our eyes have to point toward each other slightly, our brain senses this convergence and uses it to help gauge distance.

questions.stem: You are shown a picture of your grandfather’s face, but the eyes and mouth are blocked out. You still recognize it as a picture of your grandfather. Which type of processing best explains this example of perception?
questions.answer_text: Your mind filled in the information from the picture by drawing on your experience. This is top-down processing. The example does not reflect bottom-up processing because information is being filled in instead of an image being built from the elements present. Signal detection theory has to do with what sensations we pay attention to, not filling in missing elements in a picture. Opponent-process theory explains color vision.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences best describes the relationship between culture and perception?

options.A: Our perceptual rules are inborn and not affected by culture.
options.B: Perceptual rules are culturally based, so rules that apply to one culture rarely apply to another.
options.C: Most perceptual rules apply in all cultures, but some perceptual rules are learned and vary among cultures.
options.D: Slight variations in sensory apparatuses among cultures create slight differences in perception.

questions.answer_text: Most perceptual principles apply in all cultures. However, some perceptual sets are learned and do vary, so choices (A) and (B) are incorrect. Sensory apparatuses do not vary among cultures.

questions.stem: In a perception research lab, you are asked to describe the shape of the top of a box as the box is slowly rotated. Which concept are the researchers most likely investigating?

options.C: Placement of rods and cones in the retina

questions.answer_text: According to shape constancy, we know shapes remain constant even when our viewing angle changes. This experiment would not be investigating feature detectors, because the equipment required to measure the firing of feature detectors is not described. Placement of rods and cones in the retina would not affect perception of the top of the box. Binocular depth cues are probably not the target of the research because the researchers are not asking questions about depth.

questions.stem: In preparation for the upcoming homecoming game, the marching band is drilling on how to create different formations to spell out words including “Go Team” and “Touchdown”. Which of the following perceptual principles is the band most likely to rely on in creating the sense that they are spelling out words?
questions.answer_text: The marching band members would need to pay close attention to the sensory information available to them on the field, such as the position of the other band members near them and then use that information to “build up” to the sense that they are successfully spelling out the words. This is bottom-up processing: using sensations to build up to an overall interpretation or perception. Interposition is a depth cue involving looking for objects overlapping one another. Stroboscopic motion is involved in perceiving motion because of quickly presented still images (such as flip books), and similarity is a Gestalt principle involved in whether we see items as belonging to a group or not.

Top-down processing and bottom-up processing are both perceptual principles involved in how we create an overall perception of sensations. questions.stem: In a replication of a famous study, most participants directed to count the number of passes made by a basketball team, failed to notice that their school mascot, a bulldog, ran through the game. The most useful statistic that could be used to describe this result is the
questions.answer_text: Because the dependent variable in the study is not a numerical measure but rather a report of whether participants noticed the mascot or not, no range, median, or mean can be computed. The main way to describe the result is by reporting the percentage of participants who responded each way or the modal (most typical) response.

questions.stem: Mr. Krohn, a carpenter, is frustrated because he misplaced his hammer and needs to pound in the last nail in the bookcase he is building. He overlooks the fact that he could use the tennis trophy sitting above the workbench to pound in the nail. Which concept best explains why Mr. Krohn overlooked the trophy?
questions.answer_text: Functional fixedness would explain why Mr. Krohn did not think of another use for the trophy: to use it as a hammer. The representativeness heuristic is a rule of thumb for making a judgment that does not apply well to this example. Retrieval is a step in the memory process. Belief bias is our tendency to stick with a belief even when presented with evidence to the contrary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of the use of the representativeness heuristic?

options.A: Judging that a young person is more likely to be the instigator of an argument than an older person because you believe younger people are more likely to start fights
options.B: Breaking down a math story problem into smaller, representative parts in order to solve it
options.C: Judging a situation by a rule that is usually, but not always, true
options.D: Solving a problem with a rule that guarantees the right, more representative answer

questions.answer_text: The representativeness heuristic is judging a situation based on how similar the aspects are to prototypes the person holds in his or her mind. If a person has a prototype of young people as aggressive, he or she might use the representativeness heuristic to judge the situation. Breaking down the problem into smaller parts is a problem-solving technique. Judging a situation by a rule that is usually, but not always, true is a description of heuristics in general, not specifically the representativeness heuristic. An algorithm is a rule that guarantees the right answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of the use of the availability heuristic?

options.A: Judging a situation by a rule that is usually, but not always, true
options.B: Making a judgment according to past experiences that are most easily recalled
options.C: Judging that a problem should be solved using a formula that guarantees the right answer
options.D: Making a judgment according to what is usually true in your experience

questions.answer_text: By using the availability heuristic, we draw on examples that are the most readily recalled. Choice (A) is a good description of heuristics in general but not specifically the availability heuristic. Using a formula or rule that always gets the correct answer is an algorithm, so choice (C) is incorrect. Choice (D) more accurately describes the representativeness heuristic.

questions.stem: Marc is 6'7", loves sports, and Las Vegas. Given the choice, many people will say that Marc is more likely to be a professional basketball player than a high school history teacher. Such an answer results from
questions.answer_text: Marc is tall and loves sports so to many people he resembles their stereotype of a professional basketball player more than a high school history teacher. When we reason this way, by thinking primarily about similarity to a stereotype, we are using the representativeness heuristic, which often leads to errors due to people’s likelihood to ignore base rate probabilities—that is, there are way more high school history teachers than professional basketball players.

questions.stem: The door to Mr. Dorsey’s English classroom automatically shuts, and he can’t find the door stop to prop it open between classes. Samantha, one of his students, suggests he could use one of the old paperback books on his shelf. “Good idea, Samantha; I didn’t think of that!” said Mr. Dorsey. Mr. Dorsey’s difficulty stems from
questions.answer_text: Functional fixedness occurs when we fail to identify new uses for familiar objects. In this case, Mr. Dorsey didn’t think about using a paperback book as a wedge to put under the door to keep it from closing. Confirmation bias occurs when we pay more attention to evidence that supports our pre-existing beliefs. Mental set is a kind of concept formation process, and divergent thinking is the opposite of functional fixedness— divergent thinking occurs when we think about a situation or a problem in new ways.

questions.stem: Ally and Alex need to measure the gym to get ready for a science fair. Alex suggests using his iPhone to get a ballpark measurement, but Ally insists on using a tape measure to get the exact length and width so they can multiply it and get the exact area. The difference between their two approaches represents the difference between
questions.answer_text: An algorithm is a step by step process that guarantees an accurate answer (such as trying every key on a key ring one by one in order). Using a tape measure is also an example of an algorithm: it will likely take longer to measure each side of the gym, but it guarantees the right answer. Using an app on a phone to get a “ballpark” measurement is an example of a heuristic: a “rule of thumb” shortcut to problem solving that is often successful but may not work 100% of the time. The other cognitive concepts listed in the other answer options do not relate directly to the area-computation problem presented in the scenario.

questions.stem: The best way for Amelia to display her findings would be with

options.A: a table that lists the number of classes and percent guessed by each person.
options.B: a bar graph that contrasts the percents guessed by people who took three or fewer math classes with those who took four or more math classes.
options.C: a sentence that states the mean number of math classes and the mean percentage guessed.
options.D: a scatterplot that plots the number of math classes on one axis and the percent guessed on the other.

questions.context: Questions 7 through 9 refer to the following. Amelia wants to investigate the hypothesis that the more math classes people have taken, the less likely they are to believe that after a fair coin is tossed three times and comes up heads each time, the next coin toss will result in tails. She asks 30 people to report how many math classes they took in high school and college and then to rate the likelihood of the fourth coin toss coming up tails on a scale from 50 percent to 100 percent.
questions.answer_text: Because the data for both variables Amelia collects will be numerical (more specifically interval), she can plot each variable on an axis and represent each person’s pair of scores with a dot —this is called a scatterplot. Scatterplots are typically used to depict correlational relationships like the one Amelia is studying. Such a graph would be a more effective summary of 30 people’s scores than a table, so choice (A) is incorrect. The options described in choices (B) and (C) involve a loss of data specificity. For instance, if you know how many math classes people took, you don’t want to reduce that information into a group of three or fewer versus a group of four or more.

Amelia wants to investigate the hypothesis that the more math classes people have taken, the less likely they are to believe that after a fair coin is tossed three times and comes up heads each time, the next coin toss will result in tails. She asks 30 people to report how many math classes they took in high school and college and then to rate the likelihood of the fourth coin toss coming up tails on a scale from 50 percent to 100 percent.
questions.answer_text: The gambler’s fallacy is the belief that after a string of losses (or wins) in a game of chance, one is more likely to experience the opposite outcome to balance out things. Every time you flip a fair coin, you have a 50 percent chance of it landing on heads and a 50 percent chance of it landing on tails. Those probabilities do not change just because your last 3, 5, or 27 flips came up the same way; the gambler’s fallacy is the belief that those probabilities do change.

questions.context: Questions 7 through 9 refer to the following. Amelia wants to investigate the hypothesis that the more math classes people have taken, the less likely they are to believe that after a fair coin is tossed three times and comes up heads each time, the next coin toss will result in tails. She asks 30 people to report how many math classes they took in high school and college and then to rate the likelihood of the fourth coin toss coming up tails on a scale from 50 percent to 100 percent.
questions.answer_text: Because Amelia is not manipulating a variable but, rather, is looking at the relationship between two unmanipulated variables, her study is correlational. A case study is a research method that focuses on one or a small group of participants. Naturalistic observation is when the researcher watches the organisms in a study unobtrusively in order to obtain a realistic picture of what they do. An experimental study involves the manipulation of an independent variable.

questions.stem: Dr. Saltzman is planning the midterm exam for her cognitive psychology class. She wants to use an example of prospective memory. Which of the following examples would be best?

options.A: After swim practice, Carina reflects on the parts of the workout that were most difficult for her.
options.B: Jasmine creates a plan for how best to prepare for the math tournament at the end of the month.
options.C: Daniel studies various wrestling holds from matches on YouTube and practices using them on Adam.
options.D: Claire thinks back to the first time she went to her current dentist and the movie she watched during the examination.

questions.answer_text: Prospective memory involves remembering to do tasks, etc. in the future. Answer B is a good example: Jasmine is remembering a plan to prep for a math contest. Options A, C, and D all involve memory tasks related to the past or present.

questions.stem: To prepare for Ms. Sorise’s AP Psychology midterm, Tamara makes hundreds of flashcards with the definitions of every term they have learned. Her twin sister Johanna writes down all the main topics and then creates a mapping system to tie the various concepts together. Johanna’s system is likely to

options.A: result in a worse outcome because she is more likely to overlook some terms.
options.B: result in a worse outcome because using flashcards is better than making up your own system.
options.C: result in a better outcome but only if she spends more time studying than her sister.
options.D: result in a better outcome because it utilizes a deeper level of processing.

questions.answer_text: Deep processing is associated with more effective encoding of information into long-term memory and can increase the chances that information will be able to be retrieved when needed. Deep processing occurs when we think “deeply” (in complex and elaborative ways) about information in our working memory. Johanna’s studying method is a good example of deep processing, and since her method is more cognitively complex (“deeper”) than Tamara’s we can predict that it will result in a better outcome.

questions.stem: Ms. Pavlova is in a panic as the AP Psychology exam draws near. This is her first year teaching the class, and she wants to prove that she can be just as effective as her more experienced colleague Dr. Skinny. She creates a list for her students of the most important things they need to remember for the exam. Assuming Ms. Pavlova knows what she’s doing, which of the following describes how she would have ordered that list?

options.A: She would list all the terms in increasing order of importance.
options.B: She would list all the terms in decreasing order of importance.
options.C: She would put the most important terms in the middle of the list.
options.D: She would put the most important terms at the beginning and end of the list.

questions.answer_text: The correct answer choice, option D, acknowledges the Serial Position Effect: our tendency to remember the first and last items on a list better than items in the middle of the list. The other answer choices do not employ the serial position effect, and they do not align with other memory principles or research.

questions.stem: The better performance with List 1 is most likely due to

options.A: the greater time students were exposed to that list since they heard it first.
options.B: the use of a mnemonic device.
options.C: a practice effect through which students improved at the task.

He gives them a list of 10 toys and asks them to look around the classroom at their friends and imagine each friend with one of the toys. Immediately after, he gives them another list of 10 toys and asks them to read the list over and over. During the next day’s class, Mistral asks the students to recall both lists of toys. questions.answer_text: When they were thinking about List 1, students imagined each classmate holding a toy. This mnemonic device helped them think more deeply about each toy, increasing the chance that they would remember the toy on the recall task. The other explanations listed are unlikely to dramatically influence performance on the recall task across the whole class.

questions.stem: A friend mentions to you that she heard humans never forget anything; we remember everything that ever happens to us. What concept from memory research most directly contradicts this belief?
questions.answer_text: The concept of selective attention contradicts this statement. Selective attention determines what sensations we attend to and encode into short-term memory. Research shows that stimuli not attended to are not remembered, so we do not remember everything that happens to us. Sensory memory, long-term memory, and constructed memories do not obviously contradict the statement.

Matthew notices that some of his classmates tell him they have been reviewing for a few minutes each night (Space Method) while others tell him they intend to cram a day or two before the quiz (Cram Method). Matthew decides to compare their performance on the quiz and some of the data appear in the table below. Study Method Score on Test (percent) Cram 82 Space 90 Cram 76 Cram 92 Space 86 Cram 86 Space 82 Space 94 Space 88 Cram 80
questions.answer_text: The group that spaced out their studying clearly has a higher mean than the Cram group because their scores tend to be higher. Neither distribution has a clear mode because each score only appears once in each distribution. The scores in the Cram group are more spread out than those in the Space group, which will lead them to have both a higher range and standard deviation.

questions.stem: What will Mathew be able to conclude from this data?

options.A: Spacing out studying improved test performance in this chemistry class.
options.B: Hours spent studying was positively related to test scores on this exam.
options.C: Students who begin studying earlier are better at chemistry than those who cram.
options.D: The students who spaced out their studying did better than the students who crammed.

Matthew notices that some of his classmates tell him they have been reviewing for a few minutes each night (Space Method) while others tell him they intend to cram a day or two before the quiz (Cram Method). Matthew decides to compare their performance on the quiz and some of the data appear in the table below. Study Method Score on Test (percent) Cram 82 Space 90 Cram 76 Cram 92 Space 86 Cram 86 Space 82 Space 94 Space 88 Cram 80
questions.answer_text: The data show that students who spaced their studying performed better on the test than those who crammed. However, the data do not show that spacing out studying caused that difference. Matthew did not conduct an experiment, therefore, he cannot conclude that the timing of the studying caused the difference in performance.

questions.stem: During class one day, Mr. Jessup asks his students to remember two numbers—356 and 1129. Students are able to write these two numbers down a few seconds later when asked. Next, Mr. Jessup asks the students to subtract 356 from 1129 in their heads. Most quickly give up. These two tasks illustrate the difference between
questions.answer_text: Short-term memory is responsible for “holding” events/information for a few seconds so that we can use it if needed. Working memory is more “active;” it is the space we use to do “cognitive work” like subtraction. Sensory memory (the split-second awareness and memory of sensory events) and long-term memory are not involved in Mr. Jessup’s tasks.

questions.stem: What do long-term and sensory memory have in common?
questions.answer_text: Both long-term and sensory memory have huge capacity; all the sensory information we receive moment by moment are held for a split second in sensory memory, and all the events, information, skills, etc. we can recall or use from our past are held in long-term memory. The during of sensory memory and long-term memory are very different: sensory memory is a split second, and long-term memories can last our entire lives.

questions.stem: Simeon finds that when he crams for a test the night before, he usually does well but is almost completely unable to remember the material he studied a few weeks later. What best explains why this might happen?

options.A: The material he crams only makes it into his short-term memory.
options.B: Cramming the night before usually involves a shallow level of processing.
options.C: After a few weeks, he misremembers because memory is often constructed.
options.D: Simeon is suffering from retrograde amnesia.

questions.answer_text: Cramming the night before typically involves relatively superficial forms of processing that make recalling the information later difficult. Choice (A) is incorrect because short- term memory (STM) only lasts 20–30 seconds. So, if the information never made it out of the STM, Simeon would forget it long before the test. The idea that we construct our memories could explain some errors in memory like source amnesia but is unlikely to explain the inability to recall a topic at all. Finally, amnesia isn’t the same as not remembering something you once learned; it typically involves learning a larger amount of information and is most often due to a brain injury.

questions.stem: Ms. Esposito and Mr. Chai are working together to write a common midterm exam for their statistics classes. Ms. Esposito wants most of the questions to ask students to provide short answers of a few words to a set of questions, while Mr. Chai prefers the use of a multiple-choice format. What type of memory does Mr. Chai want to test?
questions.answer_text: Recognition involves being able to identify whether a correct answer matches an existing option. Multiple choice items are a perfect example of recognition; to get an item correct, students need to be able to determine whether one of the existing answer options matches their understanding of the most correct answer. Fill in the blank or short answer questions are Recall questions: students have to pull information from their long-term memories without having correct answers in front of them. Answer choices A and D do not relate to Mr. Chai’s tests.

questions.stem: After a recent break-up, Tommy finds himself unable to think of much going well in his life. He misses his boyfriend and finds himself remembering other times in his life that he felt rejected and alone. Tommy’s experience demonstrates that memory can be
questions.answer_text: Tommy’s experience is an example of “mood-congruent memory.” Our current mood can influence the likelihood that we will remember events that “align” with our mood. The other answer choices relate to memory in general but are not related to the example of Tommy only being able to remember other events that align with his current sorrowful mood.

questions.stem: Over the years, the Jones family took many driving vacations across the United States. Looking back, the two (now grown) children and their parents have very different memories of some aspects of these trips. These differences are most likely explained by

On one trip, 8-year-old Blake wandered away from the family and got lost in the woods. While everyone else recalls this incident, including Blake’s younger brother Sam, Blake has no memory of it. Which type of psychologist would provide the best explanation for Blake’s forgetting of this incident?
Paul takes a test in the army to see if he would make a good pilot. Such a test is a (an)
questions.answer_text: Aptitude tests aim to measure someone’s ability or potential. In this case, the test is supposed to show whether Paul has the ability to be a pilot. The test may or may not be standardized. The test is not attempting to measure Paul’s intelligence. Since Paul has not yet been trained as a pilot, the test is not an achievement test.

questions.stem: Mrs. Cho is careful to make sure that she fairly represents the whole year’s work on the final exam for her American literature class. If Mrs. Cho achieves this goal, her test will have
questions.answer_text: Mrs. Cho is concerned about the content validity of her test. A test that fairly represents all the material taught in her class has content validity. Validity, in general, measures how well a test measures what it is supposed to measure. For Mrs. Cho’s test to have construct validity, we would need to know that the test was successful in differentiating among varying levels of achievement in her class. Reliability is a measure of how consistent the scores are on a test. Test-retest reliability involves giving the same test to the same population on at least two different occasions and measuring the correlation between the sets of scores. Split-half reliability is when one test is divided into two parts and the correlation between people’s scores on the two halves is measured.

He has heard students in his morning class complain that people tell the students in the afternoon class about his test questions. He decides he needs to make two copies of the test, but he wants to make sure that they are equally difficult, so he decides to randomly assign an equal number of questions from the test bank to each class. Mr. Rosenboom’s concern is most closely related to
questions.answer_text: A test is considered valid if it measures what it is designed to measure. Types of validity include construct and predictive. In this case, Mr. Rosenboom is most interested in guaranteeing
