questions.stem: What kind of study is this?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 1–3. Dr. Cao studies children during their years in school. She is primarily interested in how children’s introversion and extraversion develop. She recruits 150 kindergarteners in her school district to be in her study and uses behavioral measures to assess their introversion/extraversion that spring and in the spring of third and sixth grade.
questions.answer_text: Since Dr. Cao recruited a group of kindergarten students now and plans on studying their introversion/extraversion in the spring and in the spring years later (in grade 3 and grade 6), this is longitudinal study: a study that researches one group of people over many years. It is not a naturalistic observation study because Dr. Cao is interacting with her participants by measuring a variable (introversion/extraversion). It’s not a case study because many participants are involved, and this is not a cross-sectional study because different age groups are not all being studied at the same time.

questions.stem: The graph below shows the average change in extraversion between kindergarten and grade 3 and between grades 3 and 6 as measured on a 50-point scale. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data?

options.A: Children become more introverted as they move through elementary school.
options.B: Extraversion levels do not change much during the elementary years.
options.C: Extraversion levels change more dramatically during the late elementary years.
options.D: Children in elementary school tend to be introverted.

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 1–3. Dr. Cao studies children during their years in school. She is primarily interested in how children’s introversion and extraversion develop. She recruits 150 kindergarteners in her school district to be in her study and uses behavioral measures to assess their introversion/extraversion that spring and in the spring of third and sixth grade.
questions.answer_text: Notice that the label on the y axis is “Change in Extraversion on 50-point scale” and that the only changes indicated in the graph are less than one point (.8 and .6). This indicates that Dr. Cao did not detect much change at all in introversion/extraversion during the elementary school years.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important ethical concern that Dr. Cao should consider?

options.A: During the course of the study, some children may move out of the district
options.B: Some children are innately more extraverted than others
options.C: The need to obtain parental consent and the children’s assent
options.D: The possibility that the study could cause lasting physical harm

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 1–3. Dr. Cao studies children during their years in school. She is primarily interested in how children’s introversion and extraversion develop. She recruits 150 kindergarteners in her school district to be in her study and uses behavioral measures to assess their introversion/extraversion that spring and in the spring of third and sixth grade.
questions.answer_text: One of the most important ethical principles for research with human participants is informed consent: participants need to consent to involvement with a research study. Since this study is using children, informed consent from parents is even more important: children can’t provide informed consent to participate in the study so obtaining parental consent is vital. Options A and B are not relevant to ethical concerns. Option D is important, but unlikely to apply to this study because Dr. Cao is only measuring existing levels of introversion/extraversion, so harm is not at all likely in this research design.

questions.stem: Elinor just gave birth to her first baby about four weeks ago. When Elinor strokes her baby’s cheek with her hand, which is most likely to be the baby’s response?

options.A: The baby will feel soothed and fall asleep.
options.B: The baby will get agitated and flap their arms in an uncoordinated manner.
options.C: The baby will feel surprised and its eyes will open wider.
options.D: The baby will turn its head toward Elinor’s hand.

questions.answer_text: Babies are born with a set of reflexes including the rooting reflex, which helps them learn to breastfeed by turning their heads toward anything that touches their cheeks. Answers A–C are not reflexes that babies are born with.

questions.stem: Spencer is his parents’ first child, and they delight in observing him as he progresses through various developmental milestones. Which of the following tasks is Spencer most likely to master first?
questions.answer_text: Motor development, especially “gross” motor skills like kicking a ball, develop more quickly than “fine” motor skills, like using a paintbrush, pencil, or toothbrush.

questions.stem: Superintendent Lopez is concerned that, despite studying a second language for six years in secondary school, the children in her district struggle to achieve proficiency. Budgetary concerns prevent her from simply adding more language classes. Given your knowledge of psychology, which of the following curriculum changes would you recommend she implement?

options.A: Assign more homework in the high school level language classes
options.B: Require students to divide their time between two languages in middle school
options.C: Reduce homework in the language classes
options.D: Shift the required language instruction to elementary school

questions.answer_text: Many developmental psychological findings support the conclusion that children learn language more quickly when they are younger (elementary age) so moving language learning from secondary to elementary school may help with language proficiency. The other suggestions in options A–C do not align with well-known psychological findings.

questions.stem: Janey is very excited about the Super Bowl and the big party her parents are having that night. Unfortunately for the guests, Janey keeps positioning herself right in front of the television so that the people on the couch behind her are unable to see. Janey’s inability to appreciate that she might be blocking others’ view is emblematic of which stage of development?
questions.answer_text: Janey may be viewing and acting in the world via “egocentrism,” the inability to view the world from the perspective of someone else. This scheme is typical of children during the preoperational stage. Janey is unable to understand or think about the perspective of someone else, so does not understand that she may be blocking the view of the TV.

questions.stem: Mitchell knocks his fishbowl off a shelf. Much to his mother’s horror, his pet fish, Ziggy, is severed in two during the fall. “Don’t worry, Mommy,” says Mitchell. “Daddy can fix it.” Mitchell’s faith in his father’s ability to fix the fish illustrates
questions.answer_text: Young children have naive views of life and death, often attributing “life” to inanimate objects (such as stuffed animals) and not understanding the irreversibility of death. Developmental psychologists call this misunderstanding about life and death “animism.” The developmental psychological principles in options B–D are not relevant to the death of Ziggy.

questions.stem: Ever since he was little, Eli played a lot of games with his grandma. Their favorites include speed chess and the word game, Scrabble. As Eli (and his grandmother) get older, we should expect that

options.A: Eli will quickly gain dominance in both games.
options.B: Eli will outpace Granny in speed chess before Scrabble.
options.C: Eli will outpace Granny in Scrabble before speed chess.
options.D: Eli will consistently lose to his grandma.

questions.answer_text: As humans age, our fluid intelligence—our ability to come up with creative solutions or problem solve quickly in new situations—fades as we become older adults. Chess often involves fluid intelligence, since players need to think about novel chess situations they haven’t encountered before. However, crystallized intelligence—our ability to use information already in our long-term memory—does not fade. Scrabble relies more on crystallized intelligence, since players need to know a large number of words and how to spell them.

questions.stem: “ Pet doggy!” exclaims two-year old Beckett. This is an example of
questions.answer_text: After the one-word stage of speech, children usually begin to communicate in two-word phrases; this usually happens at the age of about two years and is known as telegraphic speech. Options B, C, and D are all elements of language learning, but do not apply to this example.

questions.stem: How would you describe Professor Spencer’s research design?
questions.context: Use the following information to answer questions 11, 12 and 13. Professor Spencer is interested in how children overgeneralize grammatical rules and at what age these types of errors decrease. He partners with an elementary school and sits in during classroom Show and Tell in first- and third-grade classrooms for the month of March during which he records all overgeneralization errors students make.
questions.answer_text: Because Professor Spencer is contrasting two groups of children at different ages, his design is cross sectional. The study cannot be considered a field experiment, because, while it’s in the field, it’s not an experiment—no variable is manipulated by the experimenter. Spencer is studying too large a group and in insufficient depth to be a case study. Finally, the study would not be termed naturalistic observation both because the students will realize they are being observed and because Spencer is interested only in a very specific behavior.

questions.stem: What would you expect Professor Spencer to find?

options.A: No overgeneralization errors in any of the classrooms
options.B: Many overgeneralization errors in all of the classrooms
options.C: More overgeneralization errors in the first-grade classrooms
options.D: More overgeneralization errors in the third-grade classrooms

questions.context: Use the following information to answer questions 11, 12 and 13. Professor Spencer is interested in how children overgeneralize grammatical rules and at what age these types of errors decrease. He partners with an elementary school and sits in during classroom Show and Tell in first- and third-grade classrooms for the month of March during which he records all overgeneralization errors students make.
questions.answer_text: Overgeneralization errors—such as regularizing irregular verbs such as saying “I goed” instead of “I went”—are more common in younger children and typically decrease with experience.

questions.stem: Should Professor Spencer get IRB approval for his study?

options.A: No, it’s just a typical classroom activity.
options.B: No, the students are too young to consent.
options.C: Yes, there’s a dangerous level of deception involved.
options.D: Yes, all research with humans should be reviewed.

questions.context: Use the following information to answer questions 11, 12 and 13. Professor Spencer is interested in how children overgeneralize grammatical rules and at what age these types of errors decrease. He partners with an elementary school and sits in during classroom Show and Tell in first- and third-grade classrooms for the month of March during which he records all overgeneralization errors students make.
questions.answer_text: Generally speaking, all research using human participants should be reviewed. Although Professor Spencer’s study doesn’t sound especially dangerous and does not involve a lot of deception, it is always preferable to have a qualified group of people not associated with the study look it over with the goal of protecting the participants. While show and tell is a typical classroom activity, the introduction of the professor into the classroom and the fact that he is recording information for research purposes is enough reason to ask for IRB review. The students are, in fact, too young to consent to participate in the study. Part of the IRB’s job would be to decide whether to require parental consent and/or assent from the children.

questions.stem: Seven-year-old Jeri’s parents are recent immigrants who are very strict and traditional. Jeri’s teacher, Mr. Hubert, is easygoing and allows students a lot of freedom in his classroom. Combined, these two factors are part of Jeri’s
questions.answer_text: According to Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Model, our microsystem involves our immediate interactions with the most direct, immediate impact, including our interactions with our parents and teachers. The other possible answers listed in options A, C, and D are other elements of Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Model, but do not apply as well as option B to interactions with a child’s parents and teacher.

questions.stem: Three-year old Roberta accompanies her dad to a community meeting at a local library she has never been to before. If she is securely attached, how would you expect her to behave?

options.A: She will be interested in her surroundings but will remain with her father at all times.
options.B: She will explore the library but check in periodically with her father.
options.C: She will wander around the library and avoid her father until the meeting is over.
options.D: She will hide behind her father or under his chair to minimize the chance anyone notices her.

questions.answer_text: Children with secure attachments generally feel comfortable exploring their surroundings in a new situation but frequently come back to check in with their caregiver(s). An insecurely attached child is more likely to be unwilling to leave their caregiver (option A or D). Option C may indicate an avoidant attachment style (one of the types of insecure attachments) that involves children avoiding contact with their parents when possible.

questions.stem: You have a cousin named Holden who flunked out of three expensive private schools and was arrested for wandering the streets of New York using his parents’ credit card. Holden is intelligent but cannot seem to get motivated toward any career. What conflict would the psychosocial stage theory say Holden is struggling with?
questions.answer_text: Holden’s inability to stay in school and decide about goals indicates a search for identity according to Erikson.

questions.stem: Just before something scary happens in a horror film, they often play scary-sounding music. When I hear the music, I tense up in anticipation of the scary event. In this situation, the music serves as a(n)
questions.answer_text: The music before a scary event in a horror movie serves as a CS. It is something we associate with a fear-inducing event (the US). In this example, preparing to be scared is the CR and the fear caused by the event in the movie is the UR.

questions.stem: What is a reasonable conclusion based on the information provided?

options.A: Fluffy learned to swim to the top of her tank via positive reinforcement.
options.B: Fluffy came to associate Vinny’s typical behavior each morning with her breakfast.
options.C: Fluffy had the insight that each morning when Vinny touched the fish food, she was about to be fed.
options.D: Fluffy developed a cognitive map of her tank.

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 2 and 3. Every day, Vinny feeds his new fish, Fluffy, right before school. The graph below shows how many seconds elapse between Vinny picking up the container fish food and Fluffy swimming to the top of her tank over her first eight days in Vinny’s house.
questions.answer_text: This is most likely an example of classical conditioning. In the early days, Vinny sprinkled food on the water (UCS) and Fluffy came to the top to eat the food (UCR). Then, Fluffy started to associate some previously neutral stimulus that is part of Vinny’s typical behavior with the food (such as picking up the container of food) as a CS. From that point on, Fluffy came to the top of the water (CR) whenever the CS was perceived. Since this is an example of classical conditioning, options A, C, and D are not applicable.

questions.stem: Over Thanksgiving, Vinny goes to visit his Aunt Myrtle for a few days. While he’s away, his friend Ming takes care of Fluffy. Ming likes to sing to Fluffy before feeding her and sometimes uses the fish food container as a percussion instrument. When Vinny returns and resumes his typical feeding routine, Fluffy takes about six seconds to swim to the top of her tank. This behavior is evidence of
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 2 and 3. Every day, Vinny feeds his new fish, Fluffy, right before school. The graph below shows how many seconds elapse between Vinny picking up the container fish food and Fluffy swimming to the top of her tank over her first eight days in Vinny’s house.
questions.answer_text: Fluffy’s previously classically conditioned response became extinct, which occurred whenever a CS (such as grabbing the fish food container) was no longer associated with a UCS (sprinkling food on the top of the water). Since Ming uses the food container as a percussion instrument, they probably hold on to it for a while before sprinkling food. This delay “breaks” the classically conditioned association between grabbing the food container and the sprinkling of the food. Options A, C, and D are principles of conditioning, but do not apply to this example.

questions.stem: Two-year-old Kwame’s family recently moved, and their new house has a garage. After about a week, when Kwame hears the garage door in the evening, he excitedly toddles over to the front door to see his parents. One night, Kwame gets violently sick after a dinner that includes a new food: beets. He immediately develops a hatred of beets and refuses to eat them for the rest of his childhood. What explains why Kwame learned to dislike beets more quickly than he learned that the sound of the garage door meant his parents were home?

options.A: The feeling of dislike is a more powerful motivator than the feeling of liking.
options.B: Food is one of the most powerful reinforcers known to humankind.
options.C: Operant conditioning is more effective than classical conditioning.
options.D: We are predisposed to avoid foods we associate with nausea and vomiting.

questions.answer_text: This powerful example of “one trial” classical conditioning is called the “Garcia Effect.” Humans and other animals are biologically predisposed to associate food or drink with nausea after only “one trial.” Other classically conditioned responses (such as associating parents arriving with the sound of the garage door) require repeated pairing, but the Garcia effect predicts that it only takes one pairing of food or drink with nausea to produce a powerfully classically conditioned response. Options A–C are not relevant to classically conditioned responses.

questions.stem: Try as you might, you are unable to teach your dog to do a somersault. He will roll around on the ground, but he refuses to execute the gymnastic move you desire because of
questions.answer_text: Instinctive drift limits your pet’s gymnastic abilities. Instinctively, your dog will perform certain behaviors and will drift toward these rather than learning behaviors that go against his nature. Equipotentiality is the opposite position that asserts that any animal can be conditioned to do anything. Preparedness refers to a biological predisposition to learn some things more quickly than others. Preparedness explains why teaching a dog to fetch a stick is easier than teaching it to do a somersault. Chaining is when one has to perform a number of discrete steps in order to secure a reward.

questions.stem: When teaching your cat to jump through a hoop, which reinforcement schedule would facilitate the most rapid learning?
questions.answer_text: When teaching your cat to jump through a hoop, continuous reinforcement would result in the most rapid learning. New behaviors are learned most quickly when they are rewarded every time. However, once the skill has been learned, partial reinforcement schedules—which all the other choices are examples of—will make the behaviors more resistant to extinction.

questions.stem: Tina likes to play with slugs, but she can find them by the shed only after it rains. On what kind of reinforcement schedule is Tina’s slug hunting?
questions.answer_text: Tina’s slug hunting is rewarded on a variable-interval schedule. The passage of time is a key element in when she is reinforced because the slugs appear only after it rains. Since rain does not fall on a fixed schedule (e.g., every third day), she is on a VI schedule. If she were on a continuous schedule, Tina would find slugs whenever she looked. If the slugs appeared every three days, Tina would be on a fixed-interval schedule. If she needed to turn over three rocks to find a slug, she would be on a fixed-ratio schedule.

questions.stem: Just before the doors of the elevator close, Lola, a coworker you despise, enters the elevator. You immediately leave, mumbling about having forgotten something. Your behavior results in
questions.answer_text: Exiting the elevator to avoid Lola is negative reinforcement. Your behavior, leaving the elevator, is reinforced by the removal of an aversive stimulus (Lola). Remember that reinforcement (including negative reinforcement) always increases the likelihood of a behavior as opposed to punishment, which decreases the likelihood of a behavior.

questions.stem: When Tito was young, his parents decided to give him a quarter every day he made his bed. Tito started to make his siblings’ beds also and to help with other chores. Behaviorists would say that Tito was experiencing
questions.answer_text: Tito’s new bed-making and chore-doing regime indicates that he is generalizing. Just as a rat will press other levers in other cages, Tito is performing more chores in an attempt to maximize his rewards. Behaviorists minimize the role of internal motivation; they believe that the environment motivates. Spontaneous recovery would be correct if Tito began making his bed again after his parents had stopped rewarding him and he had returned to his slovenly ways. Acquisition occurred when Tito initially learned to make his bed to earn a quarter.

questions.stem: Before his parents will read him a bedtime story, Charley has to brush his teeth, put on his pajamas, kiss his grandmother good night, and put away his toys. This example illustrates
questions.answer_text: Charley needs to chain together a series of behaviors in order to get a reward (the bedtime story). Shaping is reinforcing approximations of a desired behavior, usually in an effort to teach it. Acquisition, in operant conditioning, is the learning of a behavior. Generalization is when one performs similar behaviors to those that will result in reinforcement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of positive reinforcement?

options.A: Buying a child a video game after she throws a tantrum
options.B: Going inside to escape a thunderstorm
options.C: Assigning a student detention for fighting
options.D: Getting a cavity filled at the dentist to halt a toothache

questions.answer_text: Buying a child a video game after she throws a tantrum is an example of positively reinforcing a behavior you probably do not want (the tantrum). This example raises an important point: the word posi tive in positive reinforcement refers to the addition of a reinforcer and not to the goodness or badness of the act that is being reinforced. Going inside to escape a thunderstorm and getting a cavity filled at the dentist to halt a toothache are both examples of negative reinforcement (removing something unpleasant). Assigning a student detention for fighting is an example of punishment (adding something unpleasant).

questions.stem: Lily keeps poking Jared in Mr. Clayton’s third-grade class. Mr. Clayton tells Jared to ignore Lily. Mr. Clayton is hoping that ignoring Lily’s behavior will
questions.answer_text: Mr. Clayton is hoping that ignoring Lily’s behavior will extinguish the behavior. Something that is not reinforced is put onto an extinction schedule.

questions.stem: Many psychologists believe that children of parents who beat them are likely to beat their own children. One common explanation for this phenomenon is
questions.answer_text: Many psychologists believe that children of parents who beat them are likely to beat their own children. One common explanation for this phenomenon is modeling. Modeling, or observational learning, is the idea that people or animals can learn from watching and copying the behavior of others.

questions.stem: In a famous study, a researcher showed that rats put in a maze for a set of trials without a reward suddenly completed the maze much faster once a reward was introduced. This finding shows that the rats

options.D: failed to make use of cognitive processes.

questions.answer_text: This is an example of “cognitive mapping” research. Rats able to explore a maze without reinforcement or punishment were able to complete that same maze later when rewarded. Researchers explain this finding by pointing out that the rats must have learned a mental picture—a cognitive map—of the maze in the early trials. Options B and C are elements of operant conditioning but are not relevant to this example. Option D is the opposite of the correct conclusion: the rats did make use of a cognitive process—a cognitive map.

questions.stem: Your new neighbor seems to know everything about ancient Greece that your social studies teacher says during the first week of school. You conclude that she is brilliant. You do not consider that she might already have learned about ancient Greece in her old school. You are evidencing
questions.answer_text: Your failure to consider the role of situational factors in explaining your new neighbor’s knowledge of ancient Greece is known as the fundamental attribution error. The self-fulfilling prophecy effect is when one person’s expectations affect another person’s behavior. Pluralistic ignorance is the tendency to look to others for hints about how one is supposed to act in certain situations. Confirmation bias is the tendency to focus on information that supports one’s initial ideas.

questions.stem: After your school’s football team has a big win, students in the halls can be heard saying “We are awesome.” The next week, after the team loses to the last-place team in the league, the same students lament that “They were terrible.” The difference in these comments illustrates
questions.answer_text: The students in the school are evidencing self-serving bias, which is the tendency to take more credit for good outcomes than bad ones. When the football team wins, they want to identify with them and therefore say “We are awesome.” When that same team loses, the students distance themselves from the players, explaining that “They were terrible.” Fundamental attribution error is a different attributional bias. It explains that people overestimate the role of personal factors when explaining other people’s behavior. The self-fulfilling prophecy effect is the finding that people’s expectations about others can influence the behavior of those others. The false consensus effect is another example of an attributional bias. It says that people overestimate the number of people who share their beliefs.

questions.stem: Based on the graph and your knowledge of psychology, which of the following statements best summarizes Dr. Julian’s findings?

options.A: Having an internal locus of control leads to better health.
options.B: People with an external locus of control tend to enjoy better health.
options.C: No significant relationship exists between locus of control and health.
options.D: Better health is associated with having an internal locus of control.

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 3–5. Dr. Julian is a primary care physician studying the relationship between locus of control and overall health. He measures the health of the adult patients he sees in June using a combination of blood pressure, pulse rate, and cholesterol level, and uses a 9- point measure on which higher scores are indicative of a more internal locus of control. His findings are shown below.
questions.answer_text: Dr. Julian is researching a correlation between health and locus of control. The scatter plot indicates that higher health scores are associated with higher internal locus of control scores. This is a positive correlation, indicating that options B and D are incorrect. Option A is wrong because correlation does not indicate causation.

questions.stem: With which of the issues below would an IRB reviewing this study be most concerned?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 3–5. Dr. Julian is a primary care physician studying the relationship between locus of control and overall health. He measures the health of the adult patients he sees in June using a combination of blood pressure, pulse rate, and cholesterol level, and uses a 9- point measure on which higher scores are indicative of a more internal locus of control. His findings are shown below.
questions.answer_text: There is very little risk of psychological or physical harm as a result of this study. If participants have access to their health or locus of control scores, they are unlikely to reveal anything those patients don’t already know. There is no indication deception is used in the study. But confidentiality is always an important ethical consideration, especially when health results are part of the research.

questions.stem: Dr. Julian’s colleague suggests that he add several factors to his measure of health. This suggestion is most related to Dr. Julian’s
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 3–5. Dr. Julian is a primary care physician studying the relationship between locus of control and overall health. He measures the health of the adult patients he sees in June using a combination of blood pressure, pulse rate, and cholesterol level, and uses a 9- point measure on which higher scores are indicative of a more internal locus of control. His findings are shown below.
questions.answer_text: The operational definition of health in the original study is “...a combination of blood pressure, pulse r ate, and cholesterol level.” Adding factors to the health score is a change in how health is being operationally defined. Adding factors to the health measure won’t necessarily influence generalizability, statistical significance, or chances of being accepted to a journal.

questions.stem: Janine has always hated the color orange. However, once she became a student at Princeton, she began to wear a lot of orange Princeton Tiger clothing. The discomfort caused by her long-standing dislike of the color orange and her current ownership of so much orange-and-black-striped clothing is known as
questions.answer_text: Janine is experiencing cognitive dissonance. The combination of her hatred of the color orange and her ownership of a lot of orange clothing results in a tension called cognitive dissonance. It will motivate her to reduce the tension by either changing her opinion of orange or radically altering her wardrobe. All of the other terms are made up.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of prejudice?

options.A: Billy will not let girls play on his hockey team.
options.C: Athena says she can run faster than anybody on the playground.
options.D: Mr. Tamp calls on boys more often than girls.

questions.answer_text: A prejudice is an attitude, while discrimination involves an action. Santiago has a negative attitude or prejudice toward cheerleaders. Billy and Mr. Tamp are engaging in discrimination by acting differently toward different groups of people. Athena may be either really fast or overconfident, but she is not evidencing a prejudice.

questions.stem: On the first day of class, Mr. Simpson divides his class into four competing groups. On the fifth day of school, Jody is sent to the principal for kicking members of the other groups. Mr. Simpson can be faulted for encouraging the creation of
questions.answer_text: By dividing his students into groups, Mr. Simpson fostered the development of in-group and out-group bias, the belief that members of one’s own group are superior to members of other groups. Although Jody’s aggressive behavior cannot be fully explained by Mr. Simpson’s grouping, the fact that he attacks only members of other groups suggests that out-group bias may play a role. Group polarization is the tendency of groups to take more extreme positions than those taken by their individual members. Since Jody acts alone and not as part of a group, his aggression cannot be seen as an example of deindividuation. Superordinate goals are helpful in reducing conflict between groups by making the groups’ success contingent upon their cooperation.

questions.stem: What is most likely to explain the difference in findings between the two parts of the study?

options.A: People are more likely to take an online study seriously than an in-person survey
options.B: Differences between commuters and people taking online tests
options.C: Explicit attitudes often don’t match implicit attitudes
options.D: The two studies weren’t done at the same time

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 9 and 10. Arturo is interested in why the United States has never elected a woman to be president. Over a school vacation, he goes to a busy commuter rail station and surveys people about whether they would be willing to vote for a woman for the presidency. Approximately 95 percent of the people Arturo surveys say they would be just as likely to vote for a woman for president as for a man. Arturo then sets up an online test to show whether people are more likely to associate male names with positions of leadership than female names. He advertises for respondents on several community message boards, and he finds that nearly 95 percent of people are quicker to pair male names with leadership positions.
questions.answer_text: Options A, B, and D are possible, but the question asks for the most likely explanation, which is that our explicit attitudes (such as opinions measured on a self-report survey) can be very different from our implicit attitudes (such as our tendency to associate leadership with male names due to internalized stereotypes).

questions.stem: Who is the population for the in-person survey Arturo conducted?

options.A: The people who answered his survey
options.B: The people who were at the train station when he conducted the survey

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 9 and 10. Arturo is interested in why the United States has never elected a woman to be president. Over a school vacation, he goes to a busy commuter rail station and surveys people about whether they would be willing to vote for a woman for the presidency. Approximately 95 percent of the people Arturo surveys say they would be just as likely to vote for a woman for president as for a man. Arturo then sets up an online test to show whether people are more likely to associate male names with positions of leadership than female names. He advertises for respondents on several community message boards, and he finds that nearly 95 percent of people are quicker to pair male names with leadership positions.
questions.answer_text: The population for a study is the larger group that a researcher wants to “generalize” the results to. In this study, the researcher is “... is interested in wh y the Uni ted States has never elected a woman to be president.” This research question indicates that Arturo wants know about attitudes and behaviors of all voters in the US.

questions.stem: Which of the following suggestions is most likely to reduce the hostility felt between antagonistic groups?

options.A: Force the groups to spend a lot of time together.
options.B: Encourage the groups to avoid each other as much as possible.
options.C: Give the groups a task that cannot be solved unless they work together.
options.D: Set up a program in which speakers attempt to persuade the groups to get along.

questions.answer_text: A task that requires groups to cooperate is an example of a superordinate goal. Such superordinate goals are effective in breaking down hostility between groups. Contact between antagonistic groups without superordinate goals is less successful, and simply avoiding members of the other group is unlikely to decrease the intergroup hostility. Although guest speakers may be able to influence the group members’ attitudes, they will be less effective than the use of superordinate goals.

questions.stem: On Monday, Tanya asked her teacher to postpone Tuesday’s test until Friday. After her teacher flatly refused, Tanya asked the teacher to push the test back one day, to Wednesday. Tanya is using the compliance strategy known as
questions.answer_text: Tanya made a large request and, when refused, came back with a smaller, more reasonable sounding request. This compliance strategy is known as door-in-the-face. Had Tanya brought her teacher an apple and then made her request, she would have been attempting to capitalize on norms of reciprocity, the idea that one good turn deserves another. Although Tanya is, in fact, attempting to broker a compromise and engage in some bargaining, the strategy she used has a more specific, psychological name.

questions.stem: What might explain the phenomenon noticed by Coach Price?
questions.context: Questions 13 and 14 refer to the following. Coach Price believes her varsity basketball team isn’t trying hard enough at its practices. As evidence, she shows them the table below that includes the free throw percentages for the starting five players across the last few practices as opposed to the last few games. Average Percent of Average Percent of Free Free Throws Made in Throws Made in Practices Games Cathy 65 75 LaTonia 70 72 Tina 56 60 Thalia 64 76 Deb 51 68
questions.answer_text: Social facilitation is when people perform a well-practiced task better when other people are present. The varsity players are good free throw shooters, and the presence of other people is likely to improve their performance. Groupthink is the tendency of groups to make poor decisions under conditions of high pressure because people are afraid to speak up and oppose what appears to be the group consensus. Conformity is when individuals change their behavior to fit in with a group. Group polarization is when groups make more extreme decisions than their members would have made separately.

questions.stem: Which of the following values is larger in the distribution of free throws taken during practices than in the distribution of free throws taken during games?
questions.context: Questions 13 and 14 refer to the following. Coach Price believes her varsity basketball team isn’t trying hard enough at its practices. As evidence, she shows them the table below that includes the free throw percentages for the starting five players across the last few practices as opposed to the last few games. Average Percent of Average Percent of Free Free Throws Made in Throws Made in Practices Games Cathy 65 75 LaTonia 70 72 Tina 56 60 Thalia 64 76 Deb 51 68
questions.answer_text: The range is the highest score minus the lowest score: 19 (70 – 51) for free throws made in practice and 16 (76 – 60) for free throws made during games. The median (middle number when ordered from high to low or vice versa) and mean (numerical average) are both higher in the game distribution. Neither distribution has a mode—the most commonly occurring value—because each value appears only once in each distribution.

questions.stem: Juan has a huge crush on Sally, but he never admits it. Instead, he tells all who will listen that Sally is really “into him.” Psychoanalysts would see Juan’s bragging as an example of
questions.answer_text: Juan is projecting. Instead of acknowledging the feelings he has toward Sally, he views Sally as having those feelings toward him. Were Juan to displace his feelings, he would express love for someone else or something else. Juan could sublimate by directing his energies toward honing his ice hockey skills or writing poetry. Finally, were Juan to deny his crush, when asked about it, he would continue to deny it.

questions.stem: Subash visits a psychologist who shows him a picture of a man standing on a dock and staring off into the distance. The psychologist asks Subash what the man is thinking and what he is likely to do next. The psychologist seems most interested in
questions.answer_text: The test this psychologist is using seems to be a projective test (possibly the Thematic Apperception Test, TAT, which involves clients looking at pictures and telling their “story.”) Projective tests are most frequently used by psychodynamic psychologists who interpret the stories people tell as a way to uncover what they believe may be conflicts, stresses, etc. in their unconscious minds.

questions.stem: What kind of psychologist is Stella likely to consider herself?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 3 and 4. Dr. Stella is a clinical psychologist who believes that the most important thing with which she can provide her patients is a warm and accepting environment. As part of her patient intake process, she gathers data on her patients’ initial subjective well-being and on whether or not they report getting unconditional positive regard from the important people in their lives. The data she has collected is graphed below.
questions.answer_text: Humanistic psychologists are interested in helping their clients develop into their “best” (most “actualized”) selves. One of the most important tools to accomplish this according to the humanistic psychological perspective is providing individuals with unconditional positive regard, which is similar to a “...a warm and accepting environment.”

questions.stem: Is the difference in subjective well-being between the two groups of patients statistically significant?

options.A: Yes, because it’s more than a 5% difference
options.B: No, the group means are too similar
options.C: Maybe, you need to check the descriptive statistics
options.D: Maybe, you need to check the inferential statistics

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 3 and 4. Dr. Stella is a clinical psychologist who believes that the most important thing with which she can provide her patients is a warm and accepting environment. As part of her patient intake process, she gathers data on her patients’ initial subjective well-being and on whether or not they report getting unconditional positive regard from the important people in their lives. The data she has collected is graphed below.
questions.answer_text: The bar graph indicates a difference between the unconditional positive regard (UPR) and non-unconditional positive regard (No UPR) groups, but in order to determine whether this difference is statistically significant, the researchers would need to use inferential statistics. These statistical techniques are designed to determine whether a difference between groups is likely to be due to the independent variable or random factors.

questions.stem: According to the data, individualistic and collectivist cultures differ most in terms of
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 5–7. Neuroticism (emotional Culture Conscientiousness Agreeableness stability) Openness Extraversion M SD M SD M SD M SD M SD Individualist 5.8 .8 4.7 .5 3.6 .6 5.4 .6 5.3 .7 Collectivist 5.7 .2 6.2 .6 3.5 .9 5.0 .8 4.9 .7
questions.answer_text: Examining the means in the data table reveals that the difference in means between the individualist and collectivist groups are the most different in the area of Agreeableness (4.7 and 6.2). The means of the groups are more similar in all the other areas.

questions.stem: Which group-trait combination resulted in the most consistent responses to the personality inventory?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 5–7. Neuroticism (emotional Culture Conscientiousness Agreeableness stability) Openness Extraversion M SD M SD M SD M SD M SD Individualist 5.8 .8 4.7 .5 3.6 .6 5.4 .6 5.3 .7 Collectivist 5.7 .2 6.2 .6 3.5 .9 5.0 .8 4.9 .7
questions.answer_text: The most consistent results would indicate that all the scores are similar and close to the mean (in this case, 5.7.) The table also includes standard deviation (SD) scores. Standard deviation is an indication of how far, on average, all scores are “away” from the mean. Since the standard deviation for the Collectivist-Conscientiousness group is the lowest SD (.2), that means these scores are the most consistent.

questions.stem: If Dion surveyed the same people in 10 years, would you expect his change a lot?

options.A: Yes, personalities develop and change lot over time.
options.B: Yes, at least one or two of the traits are likely to change significantly.
options.C: No, personality traits are relatively stable across the lifespan.
options.D: No, personality traits are innate and cannot be changed.

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 5–7. Neuroticism (emotional Culture Conscientiousness Agreeableness stability) Openness Extraversion M SD M SD M SD M SD M SD Individualist 5.8 .8 4.7 .5 3.6 .6 5.4 .6 5.3 .7 Collectivist 5.7 .2 6.2 .6 3.5 .9 5.0 .8 4.9 .7
questions.answer_text: Reliable and valid personality tests (such as the “Big 5” personality tests that measure conscientiousness, agreeableness, neuroticism, openness, and extraversion) are generally stable over the lifespan, but they often change at least slightly over time.

questions.stem: Cettina fills out a personality inventory several times over the course of one year. The results of each administration of the test are extremely different. Cettina’s situation suggests that this personality inventory may not be
questions.answer_text: A test that does not yield consistent results is not reliable. Such a test may still have been standardized and normed, both of which mean that it has been pretested on a large population and structured so that certain percentages of people answer each question in certain ways. Projective tests are used by psychoanalysts to try to see what is in a person’s unconscious.

questions.stem: How would the drive reduction theory explain a person accepting a new job with a higher salary but that requires more work and responsibility?

options.A: Money is a more powerful incentive for this individual than free time.
options.B: This person seeks a higher activity level and takes the job in order to satisfy this drive.
options.C: For this person, money is a higher-level need than free time.
options.D: The person takes the job to satisfy the secondary drive of increased salary.

questions.answer_text: Money is a secondary drive people learn to associate with primary drives. Choice (A) refers to incentive theory, choice (B) refers to arousal theory, and choice (C) refers to the hierarchy of needs.

questions.stem: What is the principal difference between how achievement motivation theory and arousal theory explain human motivation?

options.A: Achievement motivation is a specific example of arousal motivation.
options.B: Arousal theory describes the optimum level of general arousal an individual seeks, while achievement motivation describes what type of goals the individual is motivated to achieve.
options.C: Arousal theory describes motivation by referring to stages in our responses to stress (the general adaptation syndrome), while achievement motivation is not used to describe motivation due to stress.
options.D: A person with a low optimum level of arousal according to arousal theory would have a high achievement motivation.

questions.answer_text: Arousal theory says that humans are motivated to seek a certain level of arousal. Achievement motivation theory describes how we are motivated to meet goals and master our environment. The rest of the choices describe the theories incorrectly.

questions.stem: Which of the following are reasons why intrinsic motivation might be more advantageous than extrinsic motivation?

options.A: Intrinsic motivation might be more enduring since extrinsic motivations are usually temporary.
options.B: Intrinsic motivations are easier and more convenient to provide.
options.C: Intrinsic motivations are higher on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, so we are motivated to meet them before extrinsic needs.
options.D: Intrinsic motivations are more likely to be primary drives. Extrinsic motivations are secondary drives.

questions.answer_text: An intrinsically motivated person motivates himself or herself with internal rewards like satisfaction. Extrinsic motivators like money are usually temporary, and the individual may lose motivation for the task when the motivator stops or does not increase. Intrinsic motivators are not easier to provide. In fact, inspiring people to become intrinsically motivated may be more difficult. Intrinsic/extrinsic motivation does not relate to Maslow’s hierarchy or to primary and secondary drives.

questions.stem: In which of the following hormones is Dr. Pinchasick most likely to be interested?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 4 and 5. Dr. Pinchasick is a psychiatrist who helps people struggling with their weight. She uses a combination of methods including brain scans and blood tests to monitor the physiological factors that might influence people’s weight.
questions.answer_text: Some researchers call Ghrelin the “hunger hormone” because it is an important component of the systems in our body that produce our perceptions of hunger and feelings of being full. GABA and Glutamate are brain neurotransmitters. Melatonin is a hormone, but is more involved in our sleep/wake cycle than hunger perceptions.

questions.stem: Dr. Pinchasick is looking at a PET scan of one of her patients’ brains. Which of the following regions of the brain is likely to draw her interest?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 4 and 5. Dr. Pinchasick is a psychiatrist who helps people struggling with their weight. She uses a combination of methods including brain scans and blood tests to monitor the physiological factors that might influence people’s weight.
questions.answer_text: The hypothalamus is an important part of the control system for several bodily systems, including “feeding” (hunger and feelings of satiety). The hypothalamus is involved in the processes of hormones influencing behaviors, including the impact of Ghrelin on hunger perception. The other brain areas listed are less likely to be involved in hunger perception.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate conclusion to draw based on the data?

options.A: Children across the world learn to recognize emotions at about the same age.
options.B: There was a high degree of agreement across countries.
options.C: Expressions of emotion are genetically programmed.
options.D: People are much better at recognizing emotions in some countries than in others.

questions.context: Questions 6 and 7 refer to the following. Dr. Habib is the primary investigator in a cross-cultural study of emotion across rural villages in India, Mexico, Chad, and Croatia. Her team shows thousands of children between the ages of 10 and 12 the same set of photos of people depicting the emotions of happiness, sadness, and disgust to see if a similar number of people recognize the emotions across the different countries. The data from the study is presented below. India Mexico Chad Croatia Happy 97% 95% 90% 96% Angry 93% 94% 96% 92% Disgusted 78% 80% 80% 76%
questions.answer_text: With between 76 percent and 97 percent of people agreeing on all emotions and in all countries, it is reasonable to conclude that there was a high degree of agreement. Since the data were collected from children who were already at least 10 years of age and therefore have been extensively influenced by both nature and nurture, it isn’t possible to conclude anything about when or how this information was learned. All the countries appear to perform similarly on the task, according to the data.

questions.stem: Miki meets Nicky at Six Flags while waiting in a long line for a rollercoaster. They end up in the same car, and after the thrilling ride, exchange numbers and agree to get together later in the week. Three nights later, over tacos, Miki realizes that she finds Nicky to be incredibly dull. What might explain her initial attraction to him?

options.B: Emotions have physiological and cognitive components that occur simultaneously.
options.C: Emotions are essential to the adaptation of the species.
options.D: Emotions involve the cognitive interpretation of physiological responses.

questions.answer_text: Miki and Nicky’s situation is a good example of the “two factor” theory of emotion: the idea that emotions are a combination of physiological arousal (which would be heightened by being on a roller coaster) and a cognitive label or interpretation of an experience. Options A, B, and C are possibly true statements, but do not apply as specifically to Miki and Nicky’s situation.

questions.stem: Some research suggests that the expression of several basic emotions is universal. Which would be the best evidence for this claim.

options.A: A study that showed that children in Bangkok, Nairobi, and New York, all associate smiles with happiness.
options.B: A study that showed that adults in cultures with no prior contact with other parts of the world can identify an angry face.
options.C: A study that showed that babies look longer at a smiling face than a sad face.
options.D: A study that showed that women across all continents are quicker to recognize emotions than men.

questions.answer_text: If people from cultures who have had no previous contact with each other all interpret the same facial expression as “anger,” that’s the most direct evidence that some basic human emotions might be universal (rather than culture-specific). Options A, C, and D may be related to the idea that some emotions are universal, but these pieces of evidence are not as direct or conclusive as the evidence described in answer B.

questions.stem: When Shannon lost her job, she found herself devoting more time to her family and friends. What is the best way to describe this response?
questions.answer_text: Tend and befriend is one way people deal with stressful situations like losing a job; it involves bolstering one’s social connections and relationships with others. Fight-or-flight is another common response to stressful situations, but it involves either fighting against or fleeing from the cause of the stress, which is not what this example describes.

questions.stem: Jenna recently got married. She and her new spouse moved to another state because Jenna got a significant promotion at work. Everything in her life is going just as she had hoped and she is busy and happy with her situation. Which of the following is Jenna most likely to be experiencing?
questions.answer_text: Change has been found to correlate with stress. Jenna has had a lot of change in her life recently—most of it clearly associated with good things. Eustress (as opposed to distress) is motivating stress.

questions.answer_text: According to the general adaptation syndrome (GAS), people are most likely to report being sick when they reach the final of the three phases of GAS—exhaustion. It is possible that students might be going through the first two stages—alarm and resistance—earlier in the semester. By mid-semester break, students may be in the exhaustion phase, leading to them actually recognizing/feeling the effects of stress-related illness, leading to the increased percentage of health center visits at that time. Options B, C, and D are related to emotional well being, but do not apply as directly to this scenario as answer A.

questions.answer_text: Correlations range from 0 (no correlation) to 1 or –1— equally strong correlations that denote direct and inverse relationships respectively. questions.stem: Women in the United States have a higher rate of depression than do men. Which kind of psychologist would be most likely to explain this higher incidence in terms of the pressures and prejudices that women suffer?
questions.answer_text: Sociocultural psychologists believe that mental illness is mainly caused by certain negative aspects of society such as sexism and poverty.

questions.stem: At his last appointment with his therapist, Ivan explained that since he lost his job, he has felt completely worthless and depressed. Which of the following statements would a strictly cognitive therapist be most likely to say?

options.B: “I’m going to give you a homework assignment to do three things that you used to enjoy. ”
options.C: “That’s ridiculous; no one is completely worthless.”

questions.answer_text: Cognitive therapy is often somewhat confrontational as cognitive psychologists attempt to change the irrational ways their clients think. A common problem that cognitive psychologists fight is depressed people’s tendency to globalize and internalize negative thoughts. This is evidenced by Ivan’s assertion that he is completely worthless. The statement in choice (A) would more likely be made by a psychoanalytic or psychodynamic therapist. They suggest that the roots of many problems are laid in childhood, and they stress the importance of the unconscious mind to which dreams are clues. The statement in choice (B) would most likely be made by a behaviorist as it stresses the importance of behavior. The statement in choice (D) reflects humanistic psychologists’ belief in being nondirective and reflecting back what their clients say.

questions.stem: Carla, a clinical social worker, works with young adults at high risk for suicide to improve their mindset. When asked about her favorite approaches, Carla says that she uses whatever works. Carla’s approach to therapy would best be described as
questions.answer_text: Clinical psychologists who use a variety of theoretical orientations based on which might be most effective in specific situations are called “eclectic.” Options A and B refer to specific clinical orientations but do not match Carla’s description. Option D is accurate—all therapy should be evidence-based—but isn’t specific to Carl’s statement.

questions.stem: Juan hears voices that tell him to kill people. Juan is experiencing
questions.answer_text: Perceiving sensory stimulation when none exists defines a hallucination. Delusions are irrational thoughts but do not involve a belief in the existence of sensory stimulation. Obsessions are persistent, unwanted thoughts.

questions.stem: Linda’s neighbors describe her as typically shy and mild mannered. She seems to be a devoted wife and mother to her husband and three children. Unbeknownst to these neighbors, Linda sometimes dresses up in flashy, revealing clothing and goes to bars to pick up strange men. At such times, she is boisterous and overbearing. She tells everyone she meets that her name is Jen. At other times, when she is upset, Linda slips into childlike behavior and responds only to the name Sally. Linda is suffering from a
questions.answer_text: Linda is suffering from dissociative identity disorder, a type of dissociative disorder. People diagnosed with dissociative identity disorder sometimes behave as if they are experiencing multiple identities with different personalities and habits, such as Linda’s variety of behaviors described in this scenario.

questions.stem: “I am the most important person in the world” is a statement that might characterize the views of someone with which of the following personality disorders?
questions.answer_text: Narcissism is the love of oneself. People who view themselves as the focus of the world would most likely be classified as having narcissistic personality disorder.

questions.stem: Stefan was kidnapped when he was 6 and held by his captors for 19 days before he was found and returned to his family. This experience most notably elevates Stefan’s risk for which of the following types of disorders?
questions.answer_text: Dissociative disorders, in particular, have been linked to traumatic experiences like the ones Stefan experienced. The other disorders listed may be related to stress, but not as specifically as answer choice B.

questions.stem: How would you describe Dr. Costello’s research?
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 11–13. Dr. Costello believes that childhood poverty is associated with higher levels of anxiety disorders later in life. She recruits participants in their pre-teens at a community center in an economically disadvantaged part of a city to fill out a battery of tests and surveys and contacts them every 5 years for the next 20 years to complete follow-up measures. From her analysis of the participants’ responses to her open-ended survey questions, Dr. Costello concludes that poverty increases the risk of adult anxiety by nearly 30 percent.
questions.answer_text: A study that takes place over 20 years, gathering data from the same group of participants over that time, is longitudinal. The options listed in A, B, and C are research methods terms but do not apply specifically to this example.

options.B: Her conclusions could be impacted by social desirability bias.
options.C: Confirmation bias could have influenced her interpretations of the responses.
options.D: She is likely to have been affected by the false consensus effect.

questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 11–13. Dr. Costello believes that childhood poverty is associated with higher levels of anxiety disorders later in life. She recruits participants in their pre-teens at a community center in an economically disadvantaged part of a city to fill out a battery of tests and surveys and contacts them every 5 years for the next 20 years to complete follow-up measures. From her analysis of the participants’ responses to her open-ended survey questions, Dr. Costello concludes that poverty increases the risk of adult anxiety by nearly 30 percent.
questions.answer_text: Since Dr. Costello interpreted the open-ended survey questions herself, it is possible that she unconsciously looked for evidence that confirmed her initial belief. Options A, B, and D refer to possible issues regarding data interpretation, but do not apply to this scenario as specifically as answer C.

questions.stem: Dr. Costello’s finding that poverty increases the risk of anxiety by 30 percent indicates the research
questions.context: Use the information below to answer questions 11–13. Dr. Costello believes that childhood poverty is associated with higher levels of anxiety disorders later in life. She recruits participants in their pre-teens at a community center in an economically disadvantaged part of a city to fill out a battery of tests and surveys and contacts them every 5 years for the next 20 years to complete follow-up measures. From her analysis of the participants’ responses to her open-ended survey questions, Dr. Costello concludes that poverty increases the risk of adult anxiety by nearly 30 percent.
questions.answer_text: Effect size is a measure of the “impact” or amount of change associated with the target variables in a study. The finding that poverty increases risk of anxiety by 30 percent indicates that Dr. Costello’s data shows something similar—the impact or amount of change, so this 30 percent increase could also be represented by an effect size, and it would probably be a strong or somewhat large effect size. This 30 percent increase finding does not necessarily indicate anything about the other answer choices (validity, statistical significance, or representativeness).

questions.stem: Coretta’s therapist says little during their sessions and never makes any recommendations about what Coretta ought to do. What kind of therapy does Coretta’s therapist most likely practice?
questions.answer_text: Coretta’s therapist is nondirective and, therefore, is most likely to have a humanistic orientation. An example of such a therapy is Carl Rogers’s client-centered therapy.

questions.stem: Jeb has been working for the same company for three years. Although his responsibilities have increased, his salary has not. Every time he resolves to talk with his supervisor about a raise, he loses his nerve. In therapy, Dr. Flores and her assistant demonstrate how Jeb might go about asking for a raise. Then the assistant pretends to be Jeb’s boss, and Jeb practices asking for a raise. This process most closely resembles
questions.answer_text: Modeling consists of observation and imitation. Jeb first watches someone model how to ask for a raise, and then he practices that skill himself.

questions.stem: One difference between psychodynamic and cognitive modes of treatment is that cognitive therapists

options.D: view repressed thoughts about one’s childhood as the root of most problems.

questions.answer_text: Psychoanalysis stresses the importance of early childhood experience. Psychoanalysts spend a lot of time exploring patients’ early lives. Cognitive therapists focus on helping their clients deal with the present. Neither type of therapist is particularly reticent; humanistic therapists are. Neither psychoanalysts nor cognitive therapists emphasize the importance of behavior; that focus characterizes behaviorists. Psychoanalysts, not cognitive psychologists, do see repressed thoughts from childhood as the root of most adult problems.

options.B: The treatments had a negative effect on the sample.

questions.answer_text: Choice (A) is incorrect because although everyone improved, both treatment groups improved nearly twice as much as the control group. Seeing as the treatment groups improved similarly, choice (C) is incorrect. Given that all groups improved, choice (B) is incorrect.

questions.stem: What phenomenon is illustrated by the change in distress in the control group?
questions.context: Questions 4 through 6 refer to the following. A sample of 60 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder are randomly assigned to receive cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), drug therapy, or a control group given a placebo. Before the study, they are given a standard measure of psychological distress (on which a score of 1 indicates little distress and 10 indicates tremendous distress). They complete the measure again three months after beginning their assigned therapy. Their mean ratings, divided by condition, are seen in the table below. Control CBT Medication Baseline 7.2 7.4 7.0 After 3 months 5.8 4.2 3.7
questions.answer_text: Whenever we feel or do unusually well or unusually poorly, it is likely that later measurements will be less extreme, that they will regress to the mean. Within the context of the question, people are more likely to seek help with their depression when it is very severe. For instance, someone who would usually report being at a 5 on the scale is more likely to go for treatment at a moment in time they are feeling at a 7 or 8 rather than staying at a 5. Therefore, that person may feel better a few months later even without treatment because the natural course of life is that, over time, things tend to drift back toward the mean.

questions.stem: Why is it preferable to randomly assign people to treatments rather than let them choose what they prefer?

options.A: Psychologists have important medical expertise so they should do the assignment.
options.B: People may choose treatments without considering all the important factors.
options.D: Random assignment enables researchers to show cause- effect relationships.

questions.context: Questions 4 through 6 refer to the following. A sample of 60 people diagnosed with major depressive disorder are randomly assigned to receive cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), drug therapy, or a control group given a placebo. Before the study, they are given a standard measure of psychological distress (on which a score of 1 indicates little distress and 10 indicates tremendous distress). They complete the measure again three months after beginning their assigned therapy. Their mean ratings, divided by condition, are seen in the table below. Control CBT Medication Baseline 7.2 7.4 7.0 After 3 months 5.8 4.2 3.7
questions.answer_text: Random assignment is one of the hallmarks of an experiment. The goal of random assignment is to eliminate differences among the groups so that a difference in groups at the end can be ascribed to the independent variable. When people are divided into groups based on their own preferences or a researcher’s preferences, the possibility that the assignment has been affected by extraneous factors is introduced. Choice (C) is incorrect because although random samples are used to better represent populations, random sampling is a different process than the random assignment of participants to groups.

questions.stem: Gregor was a popular and successful student in high school. During his first semester of college, he begins to struggle with feelings of anxiety and inadequacy. He goes to the university’s mental health center where he begins to meet with a counselor named Shayla. Gregor quickly begins to feel like Shayla understands, listens to, and really gets him. She helps him see that he has some unrealistic expectations about college, and she works with him to identify activities that will make him happier. How would you describe Shayla’s approach to therapy?
questions.answer_text: Shayla’s therapeutic approach is most similar to the cognitive perspective on treatment. Cognitive therapists help clients like Gregor examine their own thinking—how they mentally interpret and react to the world. By helping Gregor examine his own cognitive interpretations and expectations about college and recognize what activities electricity joy/happiness/satisfaction, Shayla is helping him change how he thinks about events and memories, which may help him relieve the feelings of anxiety and inadequacy he’s experiencing. Options A–C describe other treatment perspectives, but they do not closely align with the description of Shayla’s therapy techniques.
